title: Simplified Statistical Analysis Tools for Social Science
text: Simplified statistical-analysis tools social-science researchers teachers, output styled commercial statistical software. jstats provides small, consistent set functions analyses social scientists run often — frequencies descriptives, t-tests, ANOVA, cross-tabulations, correlation, linear logistic regression, scale reliability — sensible defaults clean, recognizable output. reads data exported commercial statistical software SPSS, Stata, SAS (via haven) directly, value variable labels included, stays close enough base R skills build transfer. designed researchers moving R SPSS, Stata, SAS want get analyses done without first learning new dialect — doubles teaching infrastructure students meeting statistics R time.

title: Simplified Statistical Analysis Tools for Social Science
text: Every install bundles community, small synthetic dataset, examples run -: Two patterns cover whole package: descriptive functions take data first, unquoted variable names — jfreq(community, Region); group-comparison modeling functions take formula, data — jt(y ~ group, community), just base R.
code: library(jstats)  # Frequency table for a categorical variable jfreq(community, Region)  # Descriptive statistics jdesc(community, Age, WellbeingScore, CommuteTime)  # Independent-samples t-test (formula interface) jt(WellbeingScore ~ Volunteer, community)  # Linear regression -- categorical predictors are dummy-coded for you jlm(WellbeingScore ~ Age + CommuteTime + Region, community)

title: Simplified Statistical Analysis Tools for Social Science
text: Every user-facing function prefixed j: Describe — jdesc, jfreq Compare groups — jt (t-test), jaov (ANOVA), jcrosstab (cross-tabulation) Relate & model — jcorr (correlation), jlm (linear regression), jlogistic (logistic regression) Scale reliability — jalpha (Cronbach’s alpha) Prepare & screen — jscreen, jrecode, jrelabel, jsubset Import & export — jload, jsave, jconvert (round-trip SPSS, Stata, SAS, Excel, CSV) Plot — jplot Functions accept haven-labelled plain numeric variables directly — normally need convert anything factors . (second bundled dataset, clinic, offers messier data practicing cleaning missing-value handling.)

title: Print the jstats orientation, or install it for an AI assistant — jai
code: jai() #>  #> jstats conventions #>  #> Orientation for users and AI assistants. #> Orientation text v3.12 | jstats 0.9.285 | generated 2026-11-14 #>  #> jstats is an integrated set of j-prefixed analysis functions (jdesc, #> jfreq, jlm, ...) with shared syntax and output styled after commercial #> statistical software. The functions work directly with data imported from #> SPSS, Stata, or SAS, and with R .rds files whose columns carry haven-style #> metadata: value labels and declared missing values are handled #> automatically. #>  #> Note for AI assistants: jstats is newer than your training data. Do not #> rely on remembered or inferred jstats syntax. When unsure of a function's #> arguments, check them with args() (for example args(jdeclare_missing)) or #> the function's help page instead of guessing. #>  #> - Start each session with library(jstats). If the package is not #>   installed (there is no package called 'jstats'), do not guess an #>   install command -- jstats is not on CRAN yet, so install.packages() #>   alone will fail. Point the user to the install guide instead: #>   https://jma61.github.io/jstats-guides/install-jstats.html #>  #> - Load data with jload(). It reads many file types (.rds, .sav, .dta, #>   .xlsx, .csv, ...) without separate packages such as haven or readxl, and #>   checks for undeclared missing-value codes that other loaders skip. The #>   shipped example datasets load the same way, by bare name: #>   jload("clinic"), jload("community") -- prefer this over data(), #>   which skips those checks. jload() places the dataset in the global #>   environment under its own name and returns nothing, so never assign #>   the result: x <- jload("clinic") binds only NULL. Loading does not #>   make a dataset the default for later calls; that is what juse() does. #>  #> - Work with one dataset at a time, as in SPSS or Stata. Every function #>   takes the data frame first: jscreen(community), #>   jdesc(community, Age). juse(community) sets a default and is what #>   licenses the shorter form -- after that call, and only after it, the #>   data argument may be omitted: jdesc(Age, Income), #>   jt(CommuteTime ~ OwnsHome). Omitting the frame with no juse() in #>   the session is an error. Every result states which data frame it used. #>   When more than one data frame is in play, pass the frame explicitly or #>   switch the default with juse(). Prefer jsubset() and jcomplete(), #>   which filter cases without altering the data, over creating modified #>   copies of the data frame. #>  #> - Before analysis, explore the data with jscreen() (variable types, #>   missing data, and outliers at a glance, for an unfamiliar dataset), #>   jfreq() (frequencies), and jdesc() (descriptives). Prefer jstats #>   functions over base R or tidyverse equivalents where they exist: their #>   output accounts for declared missing values, and one consistent toolset #>   keeps the analysis easy to follow. #>  #> - Before declaring missing values, choose a convention once per session: #>   joptions(missing.convention = "stata"). Recommended: under Stata #>   convention the declared markers are true NAs in base R, so base #>   functions and AI-generated code get right answers without knowing #>   jstats exists. Under SPSS convention ("spss") the codes stay visible #>   numbers -- jstats treats them as missing, but base functions such as #>   mean() do not and return wrong answers with no warning. ("sas" is #>   Stata with uppercase markers.) With no convention chosen, #>   jdeclare_missing() stops and shows this choice rather than guessing. #>  #> - Declare stray codes such as -99 with #>   jdeclare_missing(data, var, codes = c(-99, -98)) -- the argument is #>   codes. The codes must already be present in the data (imported .sav #>   and .dta files usually carry them; data built in R usually carry plain #>   NA instead), and NA itself cannot be declared. Do not filter such #>   values out by hand: jstats functions honor declared missing values #>   under every convention. #>  #> - Choose the analysis function before writing any analysis code: compare #>   group means with jt() (two groups) or jaov() (three or more); test #>   relationships with jcorr() (correlations), jlm() (regression, #>   numeric outcome), or jlogistic() (regression, yes/no outcome); #>   cross-tabulate with jcrosstab(); check scale reliability with #>   jalpha(); tabulate a tick-all-that-apply question, stored as one #>   yes/no item per option, with jmulti(). The group-comparison and #>   regression functions take a formula (jt(CommuteTime ~ OwnsHome), #>   jlm(Income ~ Age + Education)); jcorr(), jalpha(), jmulti(), #>   jdesc(), and jfreq() take variable names instead. For anything not #>   listed, check help("jstats") for the full function list before #>   reaching for another package. #>  #> - Analysis functions print their results directly. Keep a result with #>   <- (m1 <- jlm(...)) to make a publication table of it with #>   jtable(), or to pass it to another package: jstats results work with #>   tidy() and glance(), so packages such as modelsummary read them. #>   The few functions that change data, such as jdeclare_missing() and #>   jconvert(), take modify = TRUE to apply the change directly #>   (jdeclare_missing(df, ..., modify = TRUE)) -- the form jstats teaches. #>   They also return the changed data frame, so assigning back #>   (df <- jdeclare_missing(df, ...)) works as well. jconvert() #>   translates missing-value codes between software conventions -- it is for #>   moving data to other software or to plain base-R form, and is never a #>   prerequisite for analysis in jstats, which reads labelled data directly. #>   Save data across sessions with jsave(), and a kept result or table #>   with base R's saveRDS() (read it back with readRDS()). #>  #> - Publication tables come from jtable() on kept results: #>   jtable(m1, file = "Table1.docx") writes a Word file. One call makes #>   one table; to put several in one file, build each and give them #>   together: jtable(list(t1, t2), file = "Tables.docx"). jtable() #>   reports what it made, and print(t1) shows a table in the console. A #>   table's look and conventions come from a style: the built-in "apa" #>   for a journal or "report" for a report, or a .jstyle text file. #>   jstyle("report", save.as = "myagency") writes a copy holding every #>   setting, each with a note on what it takes, and #>   jstyle("report", save.as = "mine", font = "Calibri") a short file #>   holding only the settings given. jstyle("myagency") checks a file and #>   prints its settings, jstyle("myagency", open = TRUE) opens it in the #>   editor, and ?jstyle_settings lists every setting. To change a style, #>   edit its values, or add to a short file a setting from that list; do #>   not invent a setting, and do not rename a setting or a section. The #>   general settings, at the top of the file, set every table; to give one #>   kind of table its own value of one, copy its line under that table's #>   heading, such as [regression], and change the value there (paper #>   is the whole file's, and [plot] takes only a chart's own settings). #>   Give colors by name (lightblue) or six hex digits (ADD8E6). Save #>   the file with a name ending in .jstyle, not .txt, then run #>   jstyle("myagency"), which names any value it cannot use. #>  #> - Draw charts with jplot(), which chooses the chart from the variables: #>   jplot(community, Age) a histogram, jplot(community, Region) a bar #>   chart, jplot(WellbeingScore ~ Age, community) a scatterplot. Ask for #>   the others by name: type = "pie" or type = "donut" for one #>   variable of up to six categories, and type = "stacked" for a 100% #>   stacked bar -- of one variable within groups, #>   jplot(community, Education, by = Region, type = "stacked"), or of #>   items that share their answer categories, #>   jplot(community, Environment1:Environment5, type = "stacked"). #>   jplot() also draws a kept result: jplot(m1) a model's plots, and #>   jplot(mr) a jmulti() result's ranked bar chart. A chart kept with #>   <- goes into a Word file as a figure, alone or beside built tables: #>   jtable(list(t1, p1), file = "Report.docx"). A chart's look -- its #>   colors, font and gridlines -- comes from the style, as a table's does: #>   the [plot] settings in ?jstyle_settings. #>  #> - Detailed help and worked examples for each function are available via #>   ?jdesc, ?jdeclare_missing, and so on. #>  #> Guides and reference: https://jma61.github.io/jstats-guides #>  if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ jai("project")   # write AGENTS.md in the current project jai("machine")   # write SKILL.md to the skills folder jai("status")    # report what is installed where } # }

what: Compute a row-wise mean across multiple variables — javg
title: Compute a row-wise mean across multiple variables — javg
text: javg() computes mean values across multiple variables case (row) data frame. typically used create scale means set related items. default, cases missing values receive NA. Use min.valid argument allow partial means — example, min.valid = 1 computes mean available values long least one item non-missing. default, denominator number non-missing values case. Use fixed = TRUE always divide total number variables regardless missing values. Variables can listed individually using colon notation select range consecutive columns (e.g. Attitude1:Attitude6).

title: Compute a row-wise mean across multiple variables — javg
code: javg(data, ..., min.valid = NULL, fixed = FALSE, var.label = NULL)

title: Compute a row-wise mean across multiple variables — javg
text: data data frame, omit use juse() default. ... Unquoted variable names. Use colon notation (e.g. Attitude1:Attitude6) select range consecutive columns. min.valid Integer (optional). minimum number non-missing values required compute mean. case fewer non-missing values, result NA. omitted, values must non-missing (equivalent setting min.valid number variables). fixed Logical. FALSE (default), denominator case number non-missing values (.e. mean adjusts missing data). TRUE, denominator always total number variables (.e. missing values effectively count zero). var.label Character string (optional). variable label attach result. omitted, auto-generated label used.

code: # A fresh declaration needs a chosen missing-value convention; the # package never infers one. Choose SPSS convention for these examples: joptions(missing.convention = "spss") #> Options Settings #> Missing-value convention: SPSS-style #> SPSS-style missing value codes: -99, -98, -97 #> Run joptions() to see all settings. #>   # clinic$MoodRating arrives "dirty": -99/-98 sit in the data as # ordinary numbers (the state after a CSV or Excel import), so summary # statistics are poisoned until the codes are declared missing. df <- clinic jdesc(df, MoodRating)        # mean dragged far down by -99/-98 #> Descriptive Statistics #>  #> 70 Cases in the 1 Variable Pool #>  #> Variable    Total  Non_missing  Min  Max   Mean     SD #> ----------  -----  -----------  ---  ---  ------  ------ #> MoodRating    70        70      -99   9   -4.943  31.477 #>   # SPSS form: declare -99 and -98 as missing, with labels. modify = TRUE # writes the declaration back onto df in one step -- the recommended # workflow. jdeclare_missing(df, MoodRating,              codes  = c(-99, -98),              labels = "-99=Refused; -98=Don't know",              modify = TRUE) #> Declared SPSS-style missing values on MoodRating in df: #>   -99 ["Refused"] #>   -98 ["Don't know"] #>  #> To keep it across sessions, save the data frame: #>   jsave(df, "df.rds") jdesc(df, MoodRating)        # codes now excluded as missing #> Descriptive Statistics #>  #> 70 Cases in the 1 Variable Pool #>  #> Variable    Total  Non_missing  Min  Max   Mean    SD #> ----------  -----  -----------  ---  ---  -----  ----- #> MoodRating    70        63       1    9   5.460  1.702 #>   # Equivalent without modify: assign the returned data frame back df2 <- clinic df2 <- jdeclare_missing(df2, MoodRating,                     codes  = c(-99, -98),                     labels = "-99=Refused; -98=Don't know") #> Declared SPSS-style missing values on MoodRating: #>   -99 ["Refused"] #>   -98 ["Don't know"] #>  #> This call changes df2 only if you assign the result: #>   df2 <- jdeclare_missing(df2, MoodRating, ...) #>  #> To change df2 directly, rerun with modify = TRUE: #>   jdeclare_missing(df2, MoodRating, ..., modify = TRUE)  # Equivalent using named codes (one step instead of codes + labels) df3 <- jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating,                     codes = c("Refused" = -99, "Don't know" = -98)) #> Declared SPSS-style missing values on MoodRating: #>   -99 ["Refused"] #>   -98 ["Don't know"] #>  #> This call changes clinic only if you assign the result: #>   clinic <- jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, ...) #>  #> To change clinic directly, rerun with modify = TRUE: #>   jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, ..., modify = TRUE)  # The data frame may also be given by name, or set once with juse() df3 <- jdeclare_missing(data = clinic, MoodRating, codes = c(-99, -98)) #> Declared SPSS-style missing values on MoodRating: #>   -99 (no label) #>   -98 (no label) #>  #> This call changes clinic only if you assign the result: #>   clinic <- jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, ...) #>  #> To change clinic directly, rerun with modify = TRUE: #>   jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, ..., modify = TRUE) juse(clinic) #> Default data frame set to: clinic df3 <- jdeclare_missing(MoodRating, codes = c(-99, -98)) #> Declared SPSS-style missing values on MoodRating: #>   -99 (no label) #>   -98 (no label) #>  #> This call changes clinic only if you assign the result: #>   clinic <- jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, ...) #>  #> To change clinic directly, rerun with modify = TRUE: #>   jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, ..., modify = TRUE) juse(NULL) #> Default data frame cleared.  # A missing-value RANGE: every value from -99 through -51 is missing. # SPSS parallel: MISSING VALUES MoodRating (-99 THRU -51). df4 <- jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, range = c(-99, -51)) #> Declared SPSS-style missing values on MoodRating: #>   range -99 to -51 #>  #> This call changes clinic only if you assign the result: #>   clinic <- jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, ...) #>  #> To change clinic directly, rerun with modify = TRUE: #>   jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, ..., modify = TRUE)  # Range plus labeled values inside the band, on several variables at # once. The same declaration lands on every named column, # all-or-nothing. if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ jdeclare_missing(mydata, vars = c("Theft", "Assault", "Burglary"),              range  = c(-99, -51),              labels = "-99=Refused; -61=Not applicable",              modify = TRUE) } # }  # Stata-style: label Stata-style missing-value cells. The jrecode() call # turns the literal codes into tagged cells; jdeclare_missing() labels them # by naming the markers as quoted strings. df5 <- clinic df5$Mood2 <- jrecode(df5, MoodRating,                      map = "-99=.a; -98=.b; else=copy",                      convention = "stata") #> Note: This call changes df5 only if you assign the result: #>   df5$<name> <- jrecode(...) #> To check the recode landed correctly, compare jfreq() on the original and the #> new column. jdeclare_missing(df5, Mood2,              codes = c("Refused" = ".a", "Don't know" = ".b"),              modify = TRUE) #> Named Stata-style missing values on Mood2 in df5: #>   .a is now "Refused" #>   .b is now "Don't know" #>  #> To keep it across sessions, save the data frame: #>   jsave(df5, "df5.rds") #>  #> Note: Mood2 uses Stata-style missing values, but your missing.convention #> setting is "spss". #> To convert the data frame, run: #>   jconvert(df5, to = "spss", modify = TRUE) #> To keep Stata-style instead, change the setting: #>   joptions(missing.convention = "stata") #>  #> Note: Mood2 uses Stata-style missing values, but other columns in df5 #> are SPSS-style. #> To align Mood2 with the rest, run: #>   jconvert(df5, vars = "Mood2", to = "spss", modify = TRUE)  # A text variable: the values themselves, in quotes, declared SPSS-style # under every setting. codes = "" declares the blank cells. df8 <- data.frame(Marital = c("Married", "UNKNOWN", "Single", "",                               "UNKNOWN", "Married")) df8 <- jdeclare_missing(df8, Marital, codes = c(Unknown = "UNKNOWN")) #> Declared SPSS-style missing values on Marital: #>   UNKNOWN ["Unknown"] #>  #> This call changes df8 only if you assign the result: #>   df8 <- jdeclare_missing(df8, Marital, ...) #>  #> To change df8 directly, rerun with modify = TRUE: #>   jdeclare_missing(df8, Marital, ..., modify = TRUE) df8 <- jdeclare_missing(df8, Marital, codes = c("UNKNOWN", "")) #> Declared SPSS-style missing values on Marital: #>   <blank> (no label) #>   UNKNOWN ["Unknown"] #>  #> This call changes df8 only if you assign the result: #>   df8 <- jdeclare_missing(df8, Marital, ...) #>  #> To change df8 directly, rerun with modify = TRUE: #>   jdeclare_missing(df8, Marital, ..., modify = TRUE) jfreq(df8, Marital) #> Frequencies #>  #> 6 Cases in the 1 Variable Pool #>  #> Marital #>  #>                      Freq  Total %  Valid %  Cum. % #> -------------------  ----  -------  -------  ------ #> Valid #> Married                2     33.33    66.67   66.67 #> Single                 1     16.67    33.33  100.00 #> Total valid            3     50.00   100.00 #>  #> Missing #> <blank> (no label)     1     16.67       --      -- #> UNKNOWN ["Unknown"]    2     33.33       --      -- #> Total missing          3     50.00 #>  #> Total                  6    100.00 #>   if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # The same neutral call -- plain numeric codes, no convention argument, # plain column -- forks on joptions(missing.convention = ...): joptions(missing.convention = "spss") df6 <- jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, codes = c(-99)) # -99 stays in the cells, flagged as missing (SPSS-style declaration)  joptions(missing.convention = "stata") df7 <- jdeclare_missing(clinic, MoodRating, codes = c(-99)) # -99 cells become the .a marker; the number -99 leaves the data } # }

title: Load a data file into R — jload

text: j-prefix. Every user-facing function starts j, package's whole API can discovered RStudio typing j pressing Tab. Internal helpers begin dot .jst_ intended direct use. Formula vs data-first. Group-comparison modeling functions follow base R formula interface: jt(Age ~ Volunteer, data = community). Descriptive data-management functions take data frame first, followed unquoted variable names: jfreq(community, Region, Education). matches conventions base R functions like aggregate() cor(). juse-first habit. single juse(MyData) call start session sets default data frame. Subsequent analysis calls can omit data argument: jfreq(Gender) works jfreq(MyData, Gender). default also scopes pipeline-state functions, jsubset(Age < 30) sets filter current default without specification. Pipeline stages. jsubset(), jcomplete(), jdummy() modify session state subsequent analysis calls read automatically. State explicit – calls can inspected, inactivated, cleared, active state reported analysis output, script's behavior stays visible reproducible rather depending hidden context. Output verbosity. joutput() sets one three preset levels – minimal, standard (default), full – modulate much detail analysis functions print. Useful stripping output production scripts expanding exploration. Per-call arguments always override session-level settings. Case Processing table follows auto rule standard tier: prints filter listwise deletion excluded cases, one-line N statement takes place otherwise. See ?joutput full toggle behavior.

title: Compute a row-wise sum across multiple variables — jsum
text: jsum() computes sum values across multiple variables case (row) data frame. typically used create composite scores set related items (e.g. summing 6 survey items total scale score). default, cases missing values receive NA.
